title: CEO Interview with Sergiy Nesterenko of Quilter on AI PCB Layout
gist: Quilter CEO Sergiy Nesterenko pitches physics-driven reinforcement-learning AI that automates full PCB placement and routing, positioned as a 'compiler for circuit boards' rather than a geometric autorouter. Its Project Speedrun two-board Linux computer (843 components, 5,141 pins) was laid out in 27 hours of runtime plus 38.5 hours of cleanup versus a 428-hour manual quote, with no respins; current limits include through-hole vias only and no RF/high-voltage designs.

themes.theme: PCB layout as the hardware schedule bottleneck

insights.claim: Hand layout of a moderately complex PCB takes weeks and a full computer or automotive system can take months, while firmware and validation wait on it, even though fabs can turn a board in 24 to 48 hours.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Layout time, not fabrication, gates hardware iteration speed, creating demand for automation tools.
insights.quote: A fab could turn a board in 24 to 48 hours, and designing it took weeks.
insights.locator: The idea came from my time

insights.claim: For semiconductor teams, the evaluation board or validation fixture can become the schedule bottleneck once silicon is ready to test, and every respin adds another round of layout, fabrication and bring-up.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Faster board layout can compress chip bring-up timelines, a selling point to chipmakers.
insights.locator: The main problem is layout time.

insights.claim: Customers' core pain is a shortage of PCB layout capacity rooted in scarce expertise: one customer has forty engineers, a dozen who can do PCB design, and one person with thirty years of high-speed layout experience.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Talent scarcity in high-speed layout supports pricing power for automation that substitutes for expert labor.
insights.quote: One layout lead told us flatly that he can’t be scaled.
insights.locator: Most of them don’t have enough

insights.claim: Outsourcing layout to contractors adds bandwidth but requires explicit direction, so senior engineers end up supervising and fixing contracted layouts that come back wrong.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Contract layout services are vulnerable to displacement if automated layout reduces senior-engineer supervision burden.
insights.locator: Most of them don’t have enough

themes.theme: Why PCBs are harder than chip place-and-route

insights.claim: Although chip place-and-route was automated decades ago and board autorouters have existed since the 1980s, PCBs are harder to automate because they lack the regular grid, preferred routing directions, standard vias and library cells of standard-cell digital layout.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Explains why PCB layout remains a largely manual, unautomated market despite mature chip EDA.
insights.quote: People coming from silicon often assume boards are the easier case.
insights.locator: Chip place-and-route was automated decades ago

insights.claim: Existing autorouters (Situs in Altium Designer, Allegro PCB Router in Cadence, and Siemens Xpedition routing tools) are geometric maze solvers that cannot see impedance, current capacity, return paths or net coupling, so engineers must hand-translate every electrical requirement into geometric rules.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Defines the incumbent product gap Quilter targets inside the major ECAD vendors' suites.
insights.locator: Every major commercial PCB design tool includes one

insights.claim: A single missing geometric rule can produce a board that passes design rule checks yet misses its impedance targets, because DRC does not verify physics.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Physics-aware verification is a differentiator that rule-based tools structurally lack.
insights.locator: Whether a board works depends on its physics

insights.claim: Quilter framed its founding bet on AlphaGo Zero: just as reinforcement learning learned Go from rules alone in 2017, it could learn PCB layout from physics, with the layout engine trained on synthetic boards scored against physics.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Synthetic-data RL sidesteps the scarcity of proprietary training layouts, a potential moat.
insights.quote: Software solved its version of this problem with the compiler, so I started Quilter to build a compiler for circuit boards.
insights.locator: Software solved its version

insights.claim: Quilter places and routes together, computes trace geometry for target impedance from the customer's actual stackup using Simberian's Simbeor field solver, sizes traces for net current, and attaches a physics rule check report alongside DRC to every candidate.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Integrating a third-party field solver shows the product relies on partner physics engines.
insights.locator: We built Quilter from first principles

insights.claim: Engineers upload a schematic and starter board from their own ECAD tool, and within hours Quilter returns several complete layout candidates that the engineer reviews, finishes and signs off in their own tool.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Workflow complements rather than replaces incumbent ECAD, lowering adoption friction.
insights.locator: Quilter automates PCB component placement

insights.claim: Quilter positions itself as complementary to ECAD suites from Altium, Cadence and Siemens, reading and writing native Altium, Cadence Allegro, Siemens Xpedition and KiCad files, while focusing solely on layout automation.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Coexistence strategy reduces direct conflict with incumbents but leaves acquisition or feature-copy risk.
insights.quote: layout automation is the only problem we work on
insights.locator: ECAD vendors sell the autorouter

themes.theme: Project Speedrun benchmark and performance claims

insights.claim: In Project Speedrun, Quilter placed and routed a two-board Linux computer with 843 components and 5,141 pins in 27 hours of runtime versus a 428-hour manual quote from layout services, with 38.5 hours of engineer cleanup and no respins.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Implies roughly a 6x reduction in human layout hours on a complex board, the core ROI claim.
insights.quote: Quilter placed and routed its 843 components and 5,141 pins in 27 hours of runtime. Layout services had quoted 428 hours to do it by hand.
insights.locator: Project Speedrun, the first computer

insights.claim: The Speedrun boards ran Linux with LPDDR4, Ethernet, USB, HDMI and hardware-accelerated graphics, and Quilter published input files, raw output and final designs so engineers can see what cleanup changed.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Open publication of raw output is a credibility tactic aimed at skeptical hardware engineers.
insights.locator: Project Speedrun, the first computer

insights.claim: In a pre-compliance bench test by EMC consultant Ken Wyatt, Speedrun boards' radiated emissions from roughly 250 to 650 MHz ran well below a board built from NXP's reference design files.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Suggests AI layouts can match or beat reference designs on EMC, not just speed.
insights.locator: EMC consultant Ken Wyatt

insights.claim: Project Speedrun was named a finalist in the Artificial Intelligence Design category of Fast Company's 2026 Innovation by Design Awards.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Third-party recognition, mainly marketing validation.
insights.locator: Project Speedrun, the first computer

insights.claim: Quilter handles digital and mixed-signal boards up to about 5,000 pins including DDR4/LPDDR4 interfaces, dense BGAs and impedance-controlled routing, with best fit today under 48 V and 10 A.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Defines the addressable segment today: mid-complexity eval, validation and prototype boards.
insights.locator: Quilter lays out digital and mixed-signal boards

insights.claim: Quilter currently routes through-hole vias only, so boards requiring blind, buried or microvias, as well as RF and high-voltage designs, are not yet a fit; blind and buried vias are in development to open HDI designs.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: HDI support would expand Quilter into denser, higher-value boards such as phones and servers.
insights.locator: Teams usually start with the boards

insights.claim: Quilter's 2026 releases focus on reading engineer intent from design files: automated BGA fan-out shipped in May, plus calculated impedance profiles, ground net selection, and beta reading of Altium Constraint Manager rules.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Shows deeper integration with Altium first, with other ECAD tools to follow.
insights.locator: This year’s releases focus

insights.claim: Quilter prices each board by the number of pins routed, mirroring how teams pay outside layout services, and starts commercial engagements with a paid pilot on a real backlog board.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Per-pin pricing directly targets outsourced layout service budgets.
insights.locator: Commercial teams start with a paid pilot

insights.claim: Quilter runs in a managed AWS cloud by default but can be self-hosted, including fully air-gapped, and the enterprise version does not use customer designs for training, supporting adoption by Fortune 500 aerospace, defense and consumer electronics companies.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Air-gapped deployment is key for defense customers and broadens the enterprise market.
insights.locator: Commercial teams start with a paid pilot

insights.claim: Quilter, founded in 2019 and backed by Benchmark, Index Ventures and Coatue, hired signal-integrity expert Eric Bogatin as its first Technical Fellow in September.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Tier-one VC backing and domain hires signal a well-funded private challenger in PCB EDA.
insights.locator: In September, Eric Bogatin joined
